question_name: Static disassembly of the pulled U-Boot binary to trace boot_android
findings: No disassembler is installed on this machine (checked: objdump/any gcc-or-llvm toolchain, arm-none-eabi-objdump, radare2/r2, rizin, gdb, Ghidra/analyzeHeadless, IDA/ida64 -- none found via PATH lookup or a Program Files scan; Python 3.11 is present but the capstone and pwntools packages are not installed). Per instructions, nothing was installed. Actual instruction-level disassembly and call-graph tracing of do_boot_android was therefore NOT performed -- everything below is byte/string-level static analysis only (Python stdlib: struct/hex inspection + regex string extraction), not a real disassembly. Findings: (1) uboot.bin does NOT start with a U-Boot legacy image header (magic 0x27051956 absent everywhere in the file) or a bare ARM32 reset-vector branch. It starts with an ASCII 'LOADER' tag (bytes 4C4F4144 4552 2020) followed by what looks like a length/version field and a 32-byte block resembling a SHA-256 hash, then zero padding until offset 0x800. This is a Rockchip-specific wrapper header, not a raw ARM32 vector table as the task brief assumed. (2) Code/data actually begins at file offset 0x800. The first bytes there decode as recognizable AArch64 (ARM64) opcodes: `0A 00 00 14` = `B` (unconditional branch) and `1F 20 03 D5` = `NOP` -- this is 64-bit ARM machine code, not ARM32/Thumb. This is corroborated by the compiled-in default environment string 'cpu=armv8' and 'arch=arm' found via string search (RK3326/PX30 uses Cortex-A35, which runs U-Boot proper in AArch64 even though earlier SPL/TPL stages may be 32-bit) -- this materially corrects the task brief's 'likely ARM32' assumption. (3) The 4MB dump contains two near-identical copies of the same U-Boot image, offset exactly 0x200000 (2MB) apart (e.g. the 'boot_android' string appears at both 0xa2ff8 and 0x2a2ff8) -- consistent with the env's own 'partitions=...name=loader1,...;name=loader2,...' redundant-loader-slot layout, not a hidden second payload. (4) String-level context around 'boot_android'/'bootcmd' is only the plaintext default environment block (bootcmd=boot_android ${devtype} ${devnum};boot_fit;bootrkp;run distro_bootcmd;) -- no new information beyond the prior strings pass. (5) Nearby to the 'gpt'/partition-table string cluster (~0xa17ff-0xa1c98) are real U-Boot/Rockchip symbol-name-shaped strings surviving in rodata (function names, not full symbol table): android_image_load_by_partname, android_bcb_write, android_get_dtbo, gpt_restore, gpt_verify_headers, is_valid_gpt_buf, write_mbr_and_gpt_partitions, set_protective_mbr, fb_mmc_flash_write. These are all standard upstream/Rockchip-downstream U-Boot Android-boot and GPT-repair helper names (do_gpt has a documented 'gpt restore <if> <dev>' subcommand that rewrites GPT headers/tables from a backup -- this is normal, not obviously bespoke). No custom-looking function name (e.g. something like 'txcz_restore_system' or 'oem_repair_partition') was found among these surviving strings. (6) A separate, full Android AVB A/B command surface exists ('bootavb' with slot_active/slot_unbootable/slot_successful/read_rollback/write_rollback/read_lock_status/part_size/part_guid/readabmisc subcommands) -- standard AVB tooling, not evidence of a golden-image restore. (7) No 'ext4write' string exists anywhere in the binary (only 'ext4load', 4 occurrences) -- U-Boot as built does not appear to have ext4-write command support compiled in, which argues against the hypothesis that boot_android (or anything else in this image) does an ext4-aware file-level restore into /system via that specific API; a raw block-level (non-filesystem-aware) overwrite of the partition is not ruled out by this. (8) No 'system.img', 'system_a', 'system_b', 'vbmeta_a/b', or 'odm' literal strings were found. 'super' appears only in flash-translation-layer/NAND-controller strings ('_min_slc_super_block', FTL version string) -- unrelated to the Android super/dynamic-partition concept; this is a false lead from a naive keyword search and is called out explicitly so it isn't mistaken for a real hit. 'backup' occurrences are all GPT-repair ('Repair the backup gpt table OK!') or TEE secure-storage ('TEEC: rkss_backup_sections', keybox/keymaster related) strings -- not an Android-partition golden-image backup. sha256/crc32/md5/checksum/verify/rollback strings present are generic FIT-image and AVB-rollback-index vocabulary, not a visibly hardcoded golden-hash comparison against a fixed constant (though a compiled-in comparison against a constant would not necessarily produce any distinctive string at all, so absence of a string here proves little). (9) As a quick, in-scope cross-reference, trust.bin (ATF+OP-TEE image) was also byte/string-inspected (no execution): it starts with an ASCII-ish 'BL3X'-style header tag rather than a bare vector table, and contains OP-TEE/BL31 strings plus 4 occurrences of 'system' and 8 of 'restore' -- these were not chased further since deep-diving trust.bin was outside this item's scope, but it is a candidate location for a pre-U-Boot actor and is flagged for a possible follow-up item.
relevance_to_our_symptoms: Partially informative but does not explain the symptom. What was found is consistent with (but does not prove) the hypothesis that a pre-userspace, pre-init.rc actor is responsible, since boot_android/do_gpt/bootavb all run before Android userspace and are exactly the class of code that would need to run to explain a revert visible in both Recovery and normal boot. However, nothing found here is direct evidence of the specific whole-partition-content restore behavior observed live (fresh inode, pristine mtime, MD5-identical to original, on every cold boot including straight-to-Recovery). Everything identified by name (android_image_load_by_partname, gpt_restore, bootavb/AVB rollback machinery) is standard/documented Rockchip or upstream U-Boot functionality used for selecting and loading boot/recovery images and repairing a corrupt GPT -- none of it is a filesystem-content restore mechanism by design, and no string evidence of ext4-write capability, a golden-image path, or a hardcoded-hash gate was found. The absence of compiled ext4write support is a meaningful (if not conclusive) point against a file-level restore happening inside this specific U-Boot image via that API; it does not rule out a raw block-level (dd-style) overwrite of the system partition, which would need actual disassembly (or a full-partition byte-for-byte hash/diff test across reboots, already noted as done at the file level for other partitions per outline.yaml) to detect. Net effect: this pass narrows the search space (rules out one plausible mechanism, ext4-aware write, as unsupported by this build) and corrects a wrong assumption in the original brief (ARM32 -> actually AArch64), but does NOT identify the actual restore mechanism.
confidence: low for the negative/positive findings about a hidden restore mechanism (no real disassembly was performed, so a compiled-in raw-block restore routine using no distinctive strings could easily be missed); medium-high specifically for the architecture correction (ARM32 assumption -> AArch64) and the dual-image-copy observation, since those rest on direct, unambiguous byte-pattern/opcode identification (NOP=D503201F, B=14000000|imm) and an exact 0x200000 offset match across many string occurrences, not inference.
sources_or_method: Method: (1) tool inventory via `command -v`/`where.exe` PATH lookups and a Program Files directory scan for objdump, arm-none-eabi-objdump, r2/radare2/rizin, gdb, Ghidra/analyzeHeadless, IDA/ida64, plus `python -m pip show capstone/pwntools` -- none found, nothing installed per constraint. (2) Python 3.11 stdlib (open/struct/re) used to: read uboot.bin and trust.bin as raw bytes; check the first bytes against the U-Boot legacy image magic 0x27051956 (big- and little-endian) at offset 0 and search the whole file for it (not found); hexdump the header region; locate the first non-zero byte after the header (offset 0x800) and manually decode a few leading 4-byte words against known fixed AArch64 encodings for B and NOP; regex-search (`[ -~]{4,}`) for ASCII strings around known offsets and for a target keyword list (boot_android, do_boot_android, ext4write/ext4load, sha256/crc32/md5/checksum/verify/restore/backup/rollback, partition-name literals, avb/AVB/bootavb/slot_, android_image_load_by_partname, gpt/gpt_restore, system_a/b, vbmeta_a/b, super, etc.) and printed byte offsets, occurrence counts, and surrounding string context. Limitations: this is NOT disassembly -- no instruction decoding beyond two hand-verified opcode words, no control-flow/call-graph recovery, no symbol table (the binary is stripped; the function-name-shaped strings found are leftover rodata/debug strings, not a live symbol table with addresses), and no way to compute the actual load/link base address needed to resolve any pointer or branch target. A compiled-in restore routine that doesn't reference any distinctive string (e.g. one operating purely on fixed LBA offsets and a hardcoded hash constant with no format string) would be completely invisible to this method.
safe_next_step: Ask the user for approval to add exactly one of: (a) `pip install capstone` (pure-Python bindings, no system install, ~a few MB, MIT-licensed) to get a real AArch64 disassembler usable from a short Python script -- lowest-friction option given Python is already present; (b) a portable radare2 Windows zip (no installer, extract-and-run) which adds a proper analysis/xref engine (`r2 -a arm -b 64 -m 0x800 uboot.bin`) and can auto-identify functions/strings-to-code cross-references; or (c) Ghidra (requires a JDK, heavier but gives a full decompiler and is the best tool for actually recovering do_boot_android's logic in readable pseudo-C). With any of these and the offsets already collected here (code start 0x800, AArch64, boot_android string at 0xa2ff8, bootcmd cluster at 0xa2ff0, gpt/android_image_load_by_partname cluster at ~0xa17ff-0xa1c98, second image copy at +0x200000), the next pass should: load the file as raw AArch64 code based at offset 0x800, look for xrefs (data-pool pointers) into the 'boot_android' string and the android_image_load_by_partname/gpt_restore rodata to locate their calling functions, and actually step through do_boot_android's disassembly/decompilation for any raw block-write (not ext4-write) call, hardcoded LBA/partition-offset constant, or hash comparison. This requires zero device interaction. A lower-effort, tool-free alternative that's still useful: extend the existing byte-level method to diff uboot.bin's rodata/text bytes 1:1 against a stock/reference Rockchip PX30 or RK3326 'evb_px30'-board U-Boot build (if one can be found via WebSearch/GitHub) to see whether the boot_android code region differs from stock at all -- a binary diff needs no disassembler and would show whether TXCZ patched this function.
risky_next_step_if_pursued: If static analysis (even with a real disassembler) cannot conclusively identify the mechanism, the only way to get definitive proof would be to instrument the actual boot process on the device -- e.g. patching bootdelay/bootcmd in the live U-Boot environment to drop to the U-Boot console and single-step or add debug prints around boot_android, or reflashing a modified uboot.bin with the suspected restore call patched out, then observing whether /system still reverts. This was NOT attempted and is explicitly out of scope for this task.
risk_level: High (brick risk) if pursued -- reflashing a hand-patched U-Boot image on a device without a confirmed-working Maskrom recovery path (per prior memory: 'Maskrom needs hardware access' was the real blocker on this exact device) risks an unbootable unit with no software-only recovery; even just interrupting bootcmd/dropping to a U-Boot console on a production build may be locked down (password/consle disabled) and is a device-touching action this task's safety constraint explicitly forbids.
